chunks: What is duty cycle. The question: What is duty cycle?
Duty cycle is the fraction of each repeating cycle during which a signal or switch is on. It is a number from 0 to 1, or 0 to 100 percent.
It tells you how long the switch is on, not how fast the cycle repeats. In a buck converter it is the control knob for the output voltage.
Picture a lamp that is on for 1 part out of every 4. It is on one quarter of the time.
Flick it fast enough that your eye blurs the flashes, and it looks about one quarter as bright.
Flick it even faster with the same on-fraction, and the average brightness stays the same. That is the difference between duty cycle and frequency.
Two periods of PWM at the same frequency but different duty cycles. The period is eight divisions; the high portion is 2, 4 or 6 divisions, giving 25%, 50% and 75%.
The frequency is identical in all three; only the width changes.
Period ( T ): the time of one full on-off cycle. Frequency ( f ): how many cycles per second, f equals 1 over T . On-time ( t on ): how long the switch is on within one period.
Duty cycle ( D ): D equals t on over T . PWM: pulse-width modulation, changing D to control power ("PWM and its characteristics").
A 12 volts signal switches at 100 kilohertz, so the period is 10 microseconds. It stays on for 2. 5 microseconds each cycle, so D equals 2. 5 over 10 equals 0. 25 , or 25 percent.
Its average value is 0. 25 times 12 equals 3 volts. Double the frequency to 200 kilohertz and the on-time becomes 1. 25 microseconds, but D is still 25 percent.
